doctrine:
**Reiterated:** Section 16 of RA 6758 (Salary Standardization Law) repealed charter provisions that let GOCC boards fix salaries and allowances inconsistent with the Compensation and Position Classification System, including Sections 8 and 9 of the NHA Charter (PD 757). Allowances that the DBM did not exclude from integration (CCC No. 10-99) are deemed included in the standardized salary. Meal, rice and children's allowances may continue only for employees who were incumbents, and actually receiving them, as of June 30, 1989. RATA may be paid only to positions listed in the GAA or declared of equivalent rank by the DBM. A CNA cannot justify benefits that are non-negotiable, or that are not paid as a single CNA Incentive given once after year-end from MOOE savings (DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1). **The doctrine of qualified political agency (alter ego) does not apply to Cabinet members sitting ex officio on a GOCC board, so their approval is not the President's approval.** The non-diminution principle cannot validate unauthorized benefits, however long they have been given.

Good faith cannot be appreciated (a) when a Supreme Court decision on a disallowance of the same nature already existed, or (b) when the approving officers knew facts that made the disbursement illegal. Under the **Madera v. COA** rules (reiterated), approving and certifying officers who acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence are solidarily liable to return the disallowed amounts. Recipients must return what they received unless it was genuinely given for services rendered, or unless the Court excuses the return under Rule 2d (undue prejudice, social justice, or other bona fide exceptions).

**Clarified:** the rule in **Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA**, which excuses passive recipients from refunding when three years pass between receipt and any notice of disallowance, **does not apply where the recipients signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking** acknowledging a possible refund and authorizing salary deductions for it. Those undertakings are notice of the possible illegality, so the recipients must refund even if the Notices of Disallowance came more than three years later.
facts:
On September 3, 2010, the COA formed a special audit team to examine the allowances and bonuses that the National Housing Authority (NHA), a GOCC, paid its officers, employees and board members for 2008 and 2009. In January and February 2012 the auditors issued seven Notices of Disallowance (NDs) totaling P367,844,754.36:
- cash incentive (SONA) award: P173,832,792.50
- economic subsidy: P54,954,000.00
- Christmas bonus: P71,453,000.00
- citation bonus: P14,530,000.00
- mid-year financial assistance (MYFA): P33,708,957.86
- meal, children's and rice subsidies: P18,295,504.00
- RATA: P1,070,500.00

The NDs cited Section 12 of RA 6758, MO No. 20 (2001), and Section 45 of the 2008 and 2009 GAAs. They named as liable the approving officers, the NHA Board (a majority of whom were Cabinet Secretaries), the certifying officers, and the recipients.

The liable persons relied on LOI No. 97, Sections 9 and 10 of PD 757 (NHA Charter), and Section 35, Chapter 5, Subtitle A, Title I, Book V of EO 292 (incentive awards). They also invoked the President's 1995 approval of the MYFA, non-diminution of benefits, their CNA, the alter ego doctrine (since the Board was made up of the President's alter egos), and good faith. The auditors answered that the charter and LOI had been repealed, and that the employees could not claim good faith because they had signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking.

The COA CGS-Cluster 2 Director (Decision No. 2015-013, August 13, 2015) and the COA Commission Proper (Decision No. 2018-124, January 26, 2018) affirmed the NDs. The NHA and its employees' union filed a Rule 64 petition (G.R. No. 239936). The Court allowed an amended petition after the NHA admitted it had attached the wrong NDs: those it attached covered Program Administration Fees for 2013-2014, which were still pending before the Commission Proper. After the COA issued a Notice of Finality of Decision on March 4, 2020, the NHA filed a petition for injunction (G.R. No. 252584). In a Resolution dated August 25, 2020, the Court denied the prayer for a TRO and writ of preliminary injunction in that petition.
issues: Whether the COA gravely abused its discretion in affirming the disallowance of the allowances and benefits granted to NHA officers and employees for 2008 and 2009.
Whether the approving officers and the recipients acted in good faith and should be excused from returning the disallowed amounts.
Whether the passive recipients are excused from refunding under the three-year rule of Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA.
ruling:
**1. No grave abuse of discretion; the disallowances were proper.** Grave abuse of discretion is a capricious, whimsical or arbitrary exercise of judgment so patent and gross that it amounts to an evasion of duty. The petitioners did not prove it.
- *Charter powers repealed.* Section 16 of RA 6758 repealed laws and charters that authorize allowances inconsistent with the Compensation and Position Classification System, including Sections 8 and 9 of PD 757. The DBM decides which allowances are not integrated (CCC No. 10-99). Except for RATA, none of the benefits was excluded from integration, and meal, rice and children's allowances may continue only for employees who were incumbents, and actually receiving them, as of June 30, 1989.
- *RATA* is paid only to officials whose positions are listed in Section 45 of the 2008 and 2009 GAAs or declared by the DBM to be of equivalent rank. RATA paid to other NHA employees was properly disallowed.
- *CNA.* Under DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, CNA incentives must be combined into one CNA Incentive, paid once after the end of the year and funded solely from MOOE savings. The NHA split them into several allowances paid on different dates, with no proof that they came from savings. Increases in salary and allowances not provided by law, and rice and other subsidies, are not negotiable (Resolution No. 02, s. 2003; PSLMC Resolution No. 02, s. 2004).
- *Alter ego.* The doctrine of qualified political agency cannot be extended to Cabinet members sitting on the NHA Board. Following Manalang-Demigillo v. TIDCORP, it cannot be invoked when Cabinet members act ex officio as members of a board constituted by law.
- *MYFA and Christmas bonus* are year-end benefits governed by MO No. 324 (s. 1990) and DBM Budget Circular No. 2005-06. The President's December 18, 1995 approval of the MYFA did not authorize later grants or increases. Non-diminution cannot justify the MYFA because NHA compensation is governed by laws that "sanction unauthorized or irregular compensation or benefits no matter how long it has been regularly granted."
- *SONA award and citation bonus.* The incentive-award system under Section 35 of the Administrative Code must follow CSC rules, which the NHA did not show it complied with, and it does not authorize across-the-board benefits. The DBM had in fact disallowed the SONA incentive in the NHA's 2008 and 2009 corporate operating budgets.

**2. No good faith; officers and recipients must return the amounts.** Good faith cannot be appreciated where a Supreme Court decision already covers a disallowance of the same nature, or where the approving officers knew facts that made the disbursement illegal. RA 6758 and PD 1597 plainly deny the Board power to grant or increase allowances, the rules require presidential approval, and the DBM had already disallowed some items, yet the NHA kept paying them. The Board members, a majority of them Cabinet Secretaries, are expected to know the compensation rules, so they are solidarily liable under Section 103 of PD 1445. The recipients must refund what they received because they signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking authorizing salary deductions if a refund became necessary, and nothing showed they were forced to sign. The Court also noted that under RA 10149 (GOCC Governance Act of 2011), additional compensation for GOCC employees needs a GCG recommendation and presidential approval, and neither was obtained. Applying the Madera rules, there was no good faith in the release or receipt of the amounts.

**3. No, the three-year rule does not apply.** Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA held under Madera Rule 2d that, absent other circumstances, the lapse of three years between receipt and any notice of irregularity excuses recipients from refunding. The rule does not protect those who actively took part in fraudulent transactions, and it rests on the recipients' lack of notice for a long period. Here the employees "knowingly and willingly executed notarized Deeds of Undertaking" and authorized salary deductions for any refund. **These instruments gave them sufficient notice of the illegality and irregularity of the benefits, which "precludes the application of the 3-year prescriptive period."** Even though the NDs came more than three years after receipt, the passive recipients must still refund.

On the injunction petition, the Court noted that it had already denied the prayer for a TRO and writ of preliminary injunction against the Notice of Finality in its Resolution of August 25, 2020.
disposition: The consolidated petitions were DISMISSED for lack of merit, and COA Decision No. 2018-124 dated January 26, 2018 was AFFIRMED in toto. The approving and certifying officers are solidarily liable for the return of the disallowed amounts in accordance with the Notices of Disallowance. The payee-recipients are individually liable for the return of the amounts they each received.

bar_questions.q: The 1976 charter of the Philippine Rural Housing Corporation (PRHC), a GOCC, authorizes its Board to fix the allowances of its personnel. In 2023 the Board, a majority of whom are Cabinet Secretaries sitting ex officio, approved a rice subsidy and a "service anniversary bonus" for all employees. The COA disallowed the payments. The PRHC argues that (a) its charter authorizes the Board to grant allowances, and (b) since the Board members are alter egos of the President, their approval amounts to presidential approval. Rule on both arguments.

alac.answer: Both arguments fail. The charter power was repealed by RA 6758, and the alter ego doctrine does not apply to Cabinet members sitting ex officio on a GOCC board.
alac.legal_basis: Section 16 of RA 6758 repealed all laws, decrees and corporate charters that authorize or fix salaries, pay rates or allowances inconsistent with the Compensation and Position Classification System. Allowances not excluded from integration by the DBM are deemed included in the standardized salary, and meal and rice subsidies may continue only for employees who were incumbents, and actually receiving them, as of June 30, 1989. The doctrine of qualified political agency does not extend to Cabinet members who sit ex officio on a GOCC board constituted by law (National Housing Authority v. COA, G.R. Nos. 239936 & 252584, June 21, 2022, applying Manalang-Demigillo v. TIDCORP).
alac.application: (a) The 1976 charter provision letting the Board fix allowances is inconsistent with RA 6758 and was repealed by Section 16. A rice subsidy given to all employees, and not only to those who were incumbents and receiving it on June 30, 1989, has no legal basis, and neither does a bonus not authorized by law. (b) The Cabinet Secretaries approved the benefits as Board members acting ex officio, not as the President's alter egos. Their act is not the President's act and does not supply presidential approval.
alac.conclusion: Both arguments fail, and the COA correctly disallowed the payments.

bar_questions.q: A regular COA audit found that the rank-and-file employees of a GOCC received an unauthorized "economic subsidy" in 2016. The Notice of Disallowance was issued only in 2020, and nothing shows the employees took part in any fraud. (a) Absent other circumstances, may these passive recipients invoke the lapse of more than three years to be excused from refunding? (b) Would your answer change if, before receiving the subsidy, each employee had signed a notarized Deed of Undertaking agreeing to refund it if disallowed and authorizing salary deductions for that purpose?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. Absent other circumstances, the lapse of three years without notice may excuse the passive recipients from refunding. (b) Yes, the answer changes. The Deeds of Undertaking gave them notice, so the three-year rule does not apply and they must refund.
alac.legal_basis: Under Madera v. COA, recipients must return disallowed amounts unless the amounts were genuinely given for services rendered, or the return is excused under Rule 2d (undue prejudice, social justice, or other bona fide exceptions). Applying Rule 2d, Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA held that, absent circumstances the Court deems sufficient, the lapse of three years between receipt and any notice of illegality or irregularity excuses recipients from refunding, except those who actively took part in fraudulent transactions. In National Housing Authority v. COA (G.R. Nos. 239936 & 252584, June 21, 2022), the Court held that the three-year rule does not apply where the recipients signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking authorizing deductions for a possible refund, because those instruments gave them sufficient notice of the possible illegality.
alac.application: (a) The employees are passive recipients. They received the subsidy in 2016 and had no notice of any problem until the 2020 ND, more than three years later, and they are not shown to have taken part in fraud. They may be excused. (b) By signing the Deeds of Undertaking, the employees were put on guard that the subsidy might have to be returned. The reason for the three-year rule, a long period without notice, is absent, as in NHA v. COA, so they received and spent the money at their own risk.
alac.conclusion: Passive recipients may be excused under the three-year rule only if they had no notice; those who signed refund undertakings must return the amounts.

bar_questions.q: The union of a GOCC's employees concluded a Collective Negotiation Agreement (CNA) with management. The CNA gives each employee a monthly rice subsidy, a mid-year bonus and a quarterly "productivity allowance," all paid from the GOCC's general corporate funds on various dates during the year. When the COA disallowed the payments, the union argued that the CNA is a contract with the force of law between the parties, and that the benefits had been given for many years and so can no longer be withdrawn. Is the union correct?

alac.answer: No. The benefits are not valid CNA incentives, and neither the CNA nor long practice can supply a legal basis for them.
alac.legal_basis: Under DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, all cash incentives in CNAs must be combined into a single CNA Incentive, paid once after the end of the year and funded solely from savings in released MOOE (for GOCCs, from savings in their approved corporate operating budget). Increases in salary and allowances not provided by law, and rice or other subsidies, are not negotiable (Resolution No. 02, s. 2003; PSLMC Resolution No. 02, s. 2004). The non-diminution principle cannot justify unauthorized benefits, because government compensation is governed by law (National Housing Authority v. COA, G.R. Nos. 239936 & 252584, June 21, 2022).
alac.application: The CNA divides the incentives into several allowances paid at different times of the year from general funds, instead of one incentive paid after year-end from savings. The rice subsidy and the other allowances not provided by law are non-negotiable and could not be validly granted through the CNA. That the benefits were paid for years does not make them lawful, because non-diminution does not protect unauthorized compensation.
alac.conclusion: The union is not correct, and the COA properly disallowed the CNA-based benefits.

notes: Consolidated cases: G.R. No. 239936 (Rule 64 certiorari) and G.R. No. 252584 (injunction against the COA Notice of Finality). The body says the Board members bear solidary liability "for the total disallowance," while the Madera rule it quotes limits approving and certifying officers' solidary liability to the net disallowed amount; the fallo simply holds them solidarily liable "in accordance with the notices of disallowance." The NDs on Program Administration Fees (2013-2014), which were attached to the original petition by mistake, were not resolved and remained pending before the COA Commission Proper.
